transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-14
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE); Marco Diaz (Redwood SE); Priya Shah (Redwood SE); Rachel Lin (Ashford, Head of ML); Tom Herrera (Ashford, Cloud Ops); Samantha Cole (Ashford, CTO)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive focused on air-gapped delivery and offline licensing for on-prem inference. Discussed signed bundle turnstile, firmware/driver flashing cadence, KV-cache warmup strategies that work in sealed environments, and quantization compatibility for their NVLink cluster. Action items and pilot next steps captured at end.

Topics:
- Offline bundle signing & attestation
- Transport: rsync over hardened bastion, removable media checklist
- GPU driver + firmware compatibility and signed kernels
- KV cache pre-warm and checkpoint shipping
- Batching and latency tradeoffs in deduped/airgapped scenarios
- Quantization artifacts and repro considerations

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to cover the delivery flow and make sure the on-prem constraints are captured. Marco and Priya will lead the technicals.
[00:22] Rachel Lin: Thanks Lena. Our timeline is pretty tight, we need pilot infra by end of June and firm isolation — no outbound to the internet from the inference cluster.
[00:35] Marco Diaz: Got it. So work backwards: offline bundle generation, crypto signing, handoff, soil. sorry, "handoff" to your transport team, then local verification and driver validation. We propose a signed manifest plus GPG or HSM signature for the tarball.
[00:50] Tom Herrera: We prefer PKCS#7 signatures or an HSM-signed envelope. GPG is okay but we need enterprise attestation logs. Also we have an internal requirement to run firmware-rev checks before driver load.
[01:10] Priya Shah: Understood. Our standard offline flow is: build artifact in our secure CI, generate SHA256 checksums, sign the manifest with a customer-specific key (or Redwood signing token if customer wants), then produce a short attestation document you can verify with openssl or your HSM verify process. We'll include an example script.
[01:35] Samantha Cole: How do we avoid exfil? The ops team only accepts sealed USBs from approved couriers, but we also may want rsync over a DMZ via a bastion. Both options possible?
[01:50] Marco Diaz: Yes both. We typically support: 1) sealed physical media with signed manifests and a verification checklist; 2) rsync/scp through a hardened bastion using ephemeral credentials; 3) if you have an internal package mirror, we can provide the signed artifacts for internal pull-only.
[02:10] Rachel Lin: For the sealed media, will we need to flash GPU firmware locally? Our vendor team requires signed firmware images.
[02:22] Marco Diaz: You might. Driver modules and firmware or microcode sometimes need vendor-signed blobs. For NVIDIA that means verifying the driver package version and the GPU firmware microcode rev. We're not provisioning vendor firmware — you get the vendor image, but Redwood will include a compatibility matrix and guidance on order of operations to avoid kernel module mismatch.
[02:45] Tom Herrera: Do you support signed kernel modules or DKMS flows? We run a RHEL/CentOS mix and SELinux enforced.
[02:55] Priya Shah: We do. Our docs include DKMS examples and kernel module signing steps. We also recommend enabling module signature enforcement and provide the certificate to sign modules if you want.
[03:10] Rachel Lin: On the runtime side, can you explain how KV cache warmup works offline? We can't call any external warm caches.
[03:20] Marco Diaz: Absolutely. For air-gapped, we provide a "cold checkpoint shipping" approach: during model prep in your secure lab we export the kv cache priming checkpoints for expected prefixes, then bundle them with the model artifact. At runtime the Redwood runtime can fast-load the KV checkpoint into GPU memory so early token latency is reduced. It's not live caching — it's precomputed primer states.
[03:50] Rachel Lin: That sounds promising. How big are those checkpoints? We have limited NVMe on some nodes.
[03:58] Marco Diaz: Depends on sequence length and kv strategy. For a 32k context model the checkpoints for common prefixes could be multi-GB. We can estimate with a profiling run — typically we suggest shipping compressed checkpoints and a selective prefix set so you balance disk vs latency. We'll share a sizing spreadsheet.
[04:20] Samantha Cole: What about batching? In our latency-sensitive use-case we need sub-100ms 99th percentile. Batching may be harmful.
[04:32] Priya Shah: Right. In an on-prem cluster with dedicated capacity you can tune continuous batching or disable it and use smaller batch sizes. We also have a fast-path for single-stream low-latency where KV warmup helps reduce early token generation time and avoid warm-up spikes. There is a trade-off with throughput and unit cost.
[04:55] Tom Herrera: If we disable batching, how do you keep costs predictable? We don't want runaway GPU utilization.
[05:05] Marco Diaz: For Dedicated/private customers we can set scheduling policies: core reservations, per-request concurrency limits, and graceful fallback to a smaller model variant if load spikes. Also pre-warmed idle pools with autoscale bounds. We'll talk about SLOs in the pilot SOW.
[05:28] Rachel Lin: On quantization — our models are INT8 quantized for disk, but some of our evals show occasional hallucination regressions. Are quantization profiles preserved across offline bundles?
[05:40] Priya Shah: Yes we include the quantization config files in the artifact and the runtime will use the provided quant profile. However we recommend shipping a small eval prompt set so we can run a regression test locally before you flip to the quantized runtime. Quantization artifacts are deterministic but some opcode mapping can differ by kernel versions.
[06:05] Samantha Cole: Kernel versions — that's a big one. Your runtime picks optimized kernels based on hardware; in an air-gapped cluster how do you ensure the kernels are compatible?
[06:18] Marco Diaz: The runtime ships multiple kernel binaries and a selector table. For on-prem we provide a kernel matrix that maps to your driver and firmware versions. During installation the agent runs a quick compatibility check and refuses to load a kernel if checksum mismatch or kernel-ABI mismatch. That's why we need the exact OS and driver versions ahead of time.
[06:42] Tom Herrera: What about signed kernel blobs? We require UEFI secure boot and module signing.
[06:48] Priya Shah: We provide signed modules and signatures that you can verify with your MOK (Machine Owner Key) or your CA. If you require, we can also provide instructions to embed our cert into your MOK. For UEFI-related firmware we'll provide guidance but vendor firmware still comes from the hardware vendor.
[07:10] Rachel Lin: The license mechanism — how does offline license activation work? We can't allow a live call home to a Redwood license server.
[07:18] Marco Diaz: For air-gapped deployments we support two flows: 1) offline activation using signed license tokens and a nonce exchange; 2) on-prem license server that you run in isolated DMZ that validates locally against a bundle and HSM. The offline token flow works like this: you generate a nonce on the target node, export it via secure channel, we sign a license envelope for that nonce and hand it back, then you import into the node.
[07:45] Samantha Cole: Do you support time-limited tokens and revocation lists?
[07:50] Marco Diaz: Yes tokens can be time-limited and tied to a node fingerprint (MAC, TPM quote). We also provide CRL-style revocation manifests that you can sync via removable media.
[08:05] Tom Herrera: TPM quote — do you support remote attestation or will that be local?
[08:10] Priya Shah: We can include TPM attestation in the flow; typically for air-gapped setups the attestation is captured then transferred out-of-band for verification. We can also support SGX/TEE attestation if your hardware supports it and you want that root of trust.
[08:28] Rachel Lin: A quick nit — our legal team wants to ensure the signed manifest contains the exact hash algorithm and the signer's public key fingerprint.
[08:35] Marco Diaz: We'll include an RFC-style manifest: algorithm, hash, signer fingerprint, build timestamp, build-commit-id, and optional SLSA provenance.
[08:48] Samantha Cole: On the ops side, what's the recovery flow if a node fails mid-update? We want deterministic rollbacks.
[08:56] Marco Diaz: We'll provide a rollback image and signed rollback manifest. The update process is recoverable — the agent stages artifacts in an atomic directory and only switches symlink after verification. If verification fails, agent preserves the current runtime and surfaces logs.
[09:15] Tom Herrera: For performance debugging, does Redwood provide perf counters or traces we can consume internally?
[09:22] Priya Shah: Yes we ship a telemetry bundle you can run locally. In air-gapped mode the telemetry is written to local archives which you can choose to export. We avoid PII by default and provide tokenized traces.
[09:40] Rachel Lin: Is there a recommended process for driver flashing? Our vendor suggests a driver+firmware pair per node and a specific order.
[09:49] Marco Diaz: We recommend vendor order: firmware -> reboot -> driver install -> kernel module signing -> runtime deployment. We'll document step-by-step and have a checklist for the on-site team. Also recommend a small canary node to validate before cluster-wide rollout.
[10:10] Samantha Cole: Anything unusual with NVLink or RDMA enabling?
[10:15] Marco Diaz: NVLink and RDMA often require specific kernel and mlx drivers. We'll map those in the compatibility matrix. RDMA can impact MTU and network planning so include your infra and switch firmware details.
[10:30] Rachel Lin: For the KV pre-warm, how do you select prefixes to cache? We have thousands of user prompts but a small hot set.
[10:38] Priya Shah: We recommend sampling historical traffic and generating a hot-prefix set — the runtime will support prefix-lookup on startup to load those kv segments. We can also support probabilistic pre-fetching but that needs more disk.
[10:54] Tom Herrera: Regarding quantization, can you ship both FP16 and INT8 artifacts so we can A/B?
[11:00] Marco Diaz: Yes we often include multiple model variants in the bundle and a rollout policy. That way you can switch to INT8 during low-cost windows and back if you see regressions.
[11:15] Rachel Lin: Great. Are there any security docs you can share now?
[11:18] Lena Park: We'll share our air-gap installation guide, the signing playbook, and the driver compatibility matrix. Marco will attach a sample signing script and Priya will attach the kernel signing walkthrough.
[11:30] Samantha Cole: Can you also provide a sample license envelope so legal can review?
[11:33] Marco Diaz: Yes we'll provide a sanitized sample.
[11:40] Rachel Lin: Ok last question — service support during pilot. If we find a regression after patching, what's the escalation path?
[11:46] Lena Park: You'll have a named CSM and an escalation path to SEs and on-call runtime engineers. For pilots we offer 24/5 coverage and an on-call rotation.
[11:58] Samantha Cole: Good.
[12:05] Lena Park: Let's recap next steps — Marco will send signing demo + rsync playbook, Priya kernel sign doc, Lena will propose pilot dates and SOW. Customer to share inventory and confirm handoff method.
[12:22] Rachel Lin: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[12:27] Tom Herrera: Thanks.
[12:30] Samantha Cole: Cheers.

End of transcript.
